newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Schering confident for 1997 after strong Q1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Schering confident for 1997 after strong Q1.

text.p: German drugs group Schering AG on Tuesday forecast full year 1997 profits would climb by 10 to 15 percent after favourable exchange rates and takeovers paved the way to a very strong start to the year.

During the first three months of the year, Berlin-based Schering, the world's largest maker of oral contraceptives, said net profit jumped 16 percent to 152 million marks ($89.1 million) while operating profit surged 39 percent to 273 million marks.
At the same time sales climbed 21 percent to 1.465 billion marks, with domestic sales rising 31 percent while foreign sales climbed 20 percent.

In a statement Schering said positive influences would continue to affect the company's profits in the course of the year, adding: "We therefore expect profit growth of 10-15 percent for the full year."
Analysts said results largely met expectations but the market nonetheless welcomed the outlook, sending shares up one percent to close bourse dealings at 171.10 marks.

Looking ahead to the full year Schering's chief financial officer Klaus Pohle told Reuters Financial Television that the company was expecting more strong sales in its gynaecology and therapeutics divisions.
"If our profit increases the way we have seen in the first quarter, we will also raise our dividend," Pohle said.

Last year Schering presented shareholders with a nearly 30 percent dividend rise to two marks a share, letting them participate in a 46 percent jump in consolidated earnings to a record 362 million marks.

As Schering exports over 85 percent of its products, with the U.S. and Japan making up its two largest single markets, the company also benefitted from a softer mark, making German products cheaper abroad.

Among the business units "remarkably strong developments in therapeutics and fertility control-hormone therapy led to the sharp rise in sales," Schering said. Last year's takeovers of German group Jenapharm and Finnish group Leiras contributed over one third to the rise in sales, the group said.

Unlike other German drugs groups, hard-hit by Germany's new health-care budget constraints, Schering remained largely unaffected by guidelines forcing physicians to prescribe the cheapest possible drugs. "A lot of the Schering products fall under these kind of guidelines," Ronald Koehler, analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt said.

Sales of Schering's multiple-sclerosis drug Betaferon, sold under the name Betaseron in the U.S., nearly tripled to 75 million marks in Europe but remained largely steady at 77 million marks in the U.S.

Schering also said it was sticking by its forecasts for global sales to be 590 million marks this year even though analysts predicted the company would give up more market share to newly launched competitor products like U.S. group Biogen's Avonex and Israeli group Teva's Copaxone.

Analysts also welcomed Schering's intention to buy back its own shares when German law permits, saying the step would allow Schering to raise its earnings per share by having fewer shares in the market and by extension making them more valuable.
"Schering has always been a strong supporter of shareholder value and this would be a good step," BHF's Koehler said.
